explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The fourth king will be far richer than all the others. That's not a man with a nice savings account. That's a man whose couch cushions have couch cushions.

Not quite. Daniel 11:2 says the fourth king will be far richer than all the others, so he beats the whole list. Picture three rich kings, and then he walks in and makes them look like they're clipping coupons. Money is his big thing in this verse.
Greece it is. By the power of his wealth, Persia's fourth king will stir up everyone against the kingdom of Greece. Everyone, friend. That's a group chat you do NOT want to be added to.
Babylon is a name you'd expect to hear, but this verse points somewhere else. The text says his wealth stirs up everyone against the kingdom of Greece. Same wealth, different target.

Assyria is a fair guess, but that's not the name in this verse. Daniel 11:2 says the fourth king stirs up everyone against the kingdom of Greece. His wealth does the talking, and it's talking about Greece.

I see why you'd think so, but the verse says the opposite. The kingdom will not go to his descendants, and it won't have the authority he ruled with. It will be uprooted and given to others. No family inheritance here.
That's right. Daniel 11:4 says the kingdom will not go to his descendants. It's uprooted and given to others instead. A kingdom that big, and nobody in the family gets the keys.

explanations.answer: Rule his own kingdom with great authority
explanations.explanation: That's it. The commander grows even stronger than the king of the South and rules his own kingdom with great authority. That's the employee who gets promoted right past the boss. Awkward at the next meeting, I bet.

explanations.answer: Serve the king of the South loyally
explanations.explanation: The text goes another way. The commander grows even stronger than the king, and then he rules his own kingdom. Nothing in the verse has him serving anybody.

explanations.answer: Hand his army over to the North
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything like that. It says one of the commander's strengths grows even greater than the king's, and he rules his own kingdom with great authority. His army stays his business, not the North's.
Right, to seal the agreement. I seal cookie boxes all day, friend, so I know a seal when I see one. This one is a seal between two kingdoms.
Tribute isn't what the verse gives. After some years they form an alliance, and the daughter goes to the king of the North to seal the agreement. That's the reason the text states.
That reason isn't in the text. Verse 6 says she goes to the king of the North to seal the agreement. It never says she's asking for anything.
Yes! One from her family line comes against the army of the king of the North, enters his fortress, fighting and prevailing. He doesn't just knock on the gate. He walks right in.
No peace talks in this verse. The one from her family line rises up, comes against the army of the king of the North and enters his fortress, fighting and prevailing.
He does the opposite of fleeing. Daniel 11:7 says he comes against the army, enters the fortress, and prevails. This man runs toward the trouble.

Right. The text says, “He will take even their gods captive to Egypt…” and the metal images and precious vessels of silver and gold come along with them. It's a whole moving truck of the North's treasures.
Priests aren't named in this verse. It says he takes their gods captive to Egypt, with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold.
Horses don't show up in the list. Verse 8 says gods, metal images, and precious vessels of silver and gold, all taken to Egypt.
That's right. The sons stir up strife and assemble a great army, which advances forcefully, sweeping through like a flood. A flood doesn't ask permission, friend.
No council in this verse. The sons stir up strife and assemble a great army. A meeting wouldn't sweep through like a flood.
Ships aren't mentioned here. Daniel 11:10 says the sons assemble a great army, and it advances forcefully like a flood.

explanations.answer: March out in a rage to fight
explanations.explanation: Yes. In a rage, the king of the South marches out to fight the king of the North. He doesn't wait for the doorbell. He's already out the door.
That's not what the text says. In a rage, the king of the South marches out to fight. Nobody's hiding in this verse.
No gold changes hands in verse 11. The king of the South gets angry and marches out to fight the king of the North. He's looking for a fight, not a deal.
Close, but there's a catch. He will cast down tens of thousands, but verse 12 says he will not triumph. That's the guy who wins the parking spot and finds out it's reserved.

Right. When the army is carried off, the king of the South will be proud in heart and cast down tens of thousands, but he will not triumph. Winning the fight without winning the whole thing is a strange spot to be in.

explanations.answer: It will be larger than the first
explanations.explanation: That's right. The king of the North will raise another army, larger than the first, with many supplies. He lost one army and came back with a bigger one.

explanations.answer: It will be smaller than the first
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. Daniel 11:13 says the king of the North raises another army, larger than the first. He comes back bigger, not smaller.

explanations.answer: It will be the same size as the first
explanations.explanation: Not the same size. Verse 13 says the new army is larger than the first. And it comes with many supplies.
That's the word. The violent ones among Daniel's own people will exalt themselves in fulfillment of the vision, but they will fail. A big rise doesn't promise a big finish.
Triumph is the word I'd expect, but the verse gives the opposite. They exalt themselves, but the text says they will fail. Exalting yourself isn't the same as winning.
Rule is a big word, but it's not what the verse says. The violent ones will exalt themselves, but they will fail. Nobody gets a throne here.

explanations.answer: Even their best troops won't be able to resist
explanations.explanation: Yes. The forces of the South will not stand, and even their best troops won't be able to resist. When the best can't hold, you know it's a hard day.

explanations.answer: Allies from the coastlands will rescue them
explanations.explanation: No rescue shows up in this verse. The forces of the South will not stand, and even their best troops will not be able to resist. The text doesn't mention any allies.

explanations.answer: They'll drive the North back home
explanations.explanation: That's not how it goes. Verse 15 says the forces of the South will not stand. Even their best troops won't be able to resist.
That's it. He gives him a daughter in marriage in order to overthrow the kingdom. The agreement and the plan are two different things.
Chariots aren't in this verse. The king of the North reaches an agreement with the king of the South and gives him a daughter in marriage. And the verse says that's meant to overthrow the kingdom.
Verse 17 doesn't mention that. What he gives is a daughter in marriage, in order to overthrow the kingdom. No kingdom gets split.
It sounds like a clever plan, but the verse says otherwise. His plan will not succeed or help him. The marriage is meant to overthrow the kingdom, and it doesn't work.
That's right. Daniel 11:17 says his plan will not succeed or help him. All that scheming, and the plan goes nowhere.
Yes. After he turns his face to the coastlands and captures many of them, a commander puts an end to his reproach and turns it back upon him. He gets a taste of his own medicine.
Verse 18 says the opposite. A commander will put an end to his reproach and will turn it back upon him. So yes, the captures are followed by a commander who answers him.

explanations.answer: He'll stumble and fall and be no more
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. He turns back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he will stumble and fall and be no more. I think this one is heavy, friend, so let it sit for a second.

explanations.answer: He'll rebuild a greater army there
explanations.explanation: That's not what happens. He turns back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he will stumble and fall and be no more. No new army this time.

explanations.answer: He'll rule in peace for many years
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't give him a quiet retirement. After turning back toward his own land's fortresses, he will stumble and fall and be no more. It's a heavy ending.
Part of that is right, but not the end. He's destroyed within a few days, though the text says not in anger or in battle. That's the part the question changed.
Right. Daniel 11:20 says within a few days he will be destroyed, though not in anger or in battle. A few days is a very short reign.

explanations.answer: He'll seize it by intrigue in a time of peace
explanations.explanation: That's it. Royal honors won't be given to him, but he comes in a time of peace and seizes the kingdom by intrigue. No parade, no crown. He just slips in the side door.

explanations.answer: He'll win it in a great battle at sea
explanations.explanation: No sea battle in this verse. He comes in a time of peace and seizes the kingdom by intrigue. Quiet scheming is his method.

explanations.answer: The king of the South will hand it to him
explanations.explanation: Nobody hands him anything. Verse 21 says royal honors will not be given to him, and he seizes the kingdom by intrigue. He takes it himself.
That's tempting after an alliance, but the text says otherwise. After an alliance is made with him, he acts deceitfully. He rises to power with only a few people, and honesty isn't how he does it.
That's right. Daniel 11:23 says that after an alliance is made with him, he will act deceitfully. Watch who you shake hands with.
Yes. He lavishes plunder, loot, and wealth on his followers. Happiest guy at the party, if you're on his side.

explanations.answer: Hide it away in his strongholds
explanations.explanation: Verse 24 doesn't say that. He lavishes the plunder, loot, and wealth on his followers, and he plots against the strongholds. He's not hiding it away.

explanations.answer: Send it as tribute to the South
explanations.explanation: The South gets nothing from him here. The text says he lavishes plunder, loot, and wealth on his followers. They're the ones who get it.
Right. The king of the South mobilizes a very large and powerful army, but he will not withstand the plots devised against him. Biggest army in the room, outplayed by plans made behind his back.

explanations.answer: A sickness spreading through his camp
explanations.explanation: The text names something else. The king of the South will not withstand the plots devised against him. Sickness isn't in the verse.

explanations.answer: A storm that wrecks his ships
explanations.explanation: No storm in this verse. His army is very large and powerful, but verse 25 says he will not withstand the plots devised against him.
Yes. Those who eat from his provisions will seek to destroy him. It's like biting the hand that fills the cookie jar.
The verse says it is true. Daniel 11:26 says those who eat from his provisions will seek to destroy him. The trouble comes from inside his own circle.

explanations.answer: The end will still come at the appointed time
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the verse gives. The two kings speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for still the end will come at the appointed time. Their lies don't change it.

explanations.answer: Each king will see through the other's lies
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that. It says the lies are to no avail, for still the end will come at the appointed time. The reason is the appointed time.

explanations.answer: Their own officials will expose them both
explanations.explanation: Officials don't come into this verse. The two kings speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for still the end will come at the appointed time.

explanations.answer: He'll lose heart and turn back
explanations.explanation: Right. The ships of Kittim come against him, and he will lose heart and turn back. All that power, and his heart drops when the ships show up.

explanations.answer: He'll sink every one of them
explanations.explanation: That's not what happens. The ships of Kittim come against him, and he will lose heart. Then he turns back.
Verse 30 doesn't say that. The ships come against him, he loses heart, and he turns back. No teaming up.
The card flipped it around. After raging against the holy covenant, he shows favor to those who forsake the holy covenant. Not to those who keep it.
That's right. Daniel 11:30 says he will return and show favor to those who forsake the holy covenant. The favor goes to the people walking away from it.
Yes. The text says, “…the people who know their God will firmly resist him.” He corrupts with flattery, and they hold firm. That's a steady kind of strong.
Following is what the flattery is aiming for, but verse 32 says something else. The people who know their God will firmly resist him. His flattery corrupts those who violate the covenant, not them.
Fear isn't the word in the verse. It says, “…the people who know their God will firmly resist him.” They hold firm.

explanations.answer: So they may be refined and purified
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The verse says, “…so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless…” I think this part is heavy, friend, so I'll let the verse speak for itself.

explanations.answer: So their enemies may be put to shame
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't give that reason. It says some of the wise will fall so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless. I think this one hurts to read.

explanations.answer: So the city may be spared
explanations.explanation: Sparing the city isn't mentioned here. The text says, “…so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless…” It's a heavy verse, so I'll keep close to its words.
